This article focuses on the depiction of the Berlin Wall in four of his novels set in Germany. Interweaving personal and world histories, past and present, Hamilton explores relationships – with places as much as with people. In Surrogate City (1990), the narrative focuses on the character of Helen who has moved from Ireland to West Berlin, while the characters in The Love Test (1995) are from East Berlin and attempt to cross over to flee the Stasi. The protagonist of Disguise (2008) is in and out of Berlin in search of his own story and history. In Every Single Minute (2014), the narrator Liam takes his dying friend on a last touristic trip to the German capital. The corpus offers four different perspectives on the Berlin Wall that span a little over a decade in terms of publication, but nearly forty years with regards to the narratives: Surrogate City is set during the Cold War, The Love Test and Disguise alternate between chapters in a post-war, partitioned Germany and passages set in the aftermath of 1989, while Every Single Minute takes place in contemporary times. This study focuses on the depiction and significance of the Berlin Wall in the novels, from its historical role as a boundary between two worldviews, separating people, to its fall and the aftermath of it. The chronology of the novels reflects that of the Wall’s history and affects its depiction in the narratives. This geocritical study examines the fictional representation of a geographical place and the evolution of this portrayal. Simultaneously, the article argues for the use of sensorial mapping in literary analysis. Exemplifying it through the study of Hamilton’s novels, a case is made for this cartographical practice that subverts the conventions of the discipline in order to highlight emotions and impressions, making it all the more suited to literary geography and geocriticism. Maps are thus included to illustrate and reinforce the points made in this study, further challenging the boundaries between disciplines.

title: Irish Migrations and Classical Antiquity
reasons: literary/cultural analysis without data
abstract:
This open-access volume explores the reception of Graeco-Romano culture from Ireland’s earliest medieval scholars such as Columbanus and John Scottus Eriugena to later writers including James Joyce, Seamus Heaney and Colm Tóibín. Migrations and classical antiquity have played a key interconnected role for successive centuries in the experiences of the Irish diaspora, in the articulations of those experiences, as well as in the influences of Irish classicism abroad. Throughout subsequent centuries ancient Greece and Rome were repeatedly evoked in literature, art, and historiographies associated with migrations as vehicles for the expression of varied political and cultural positions.
 The chapters in this collection explore how the early Irish peregrini left their mark on continental scholarship; how the model of ancient Rome was coopted for political purposes; the ways in which Protestant writers adopted the notion of ancient Romanitas as a key to the British imperial project; and, finally, how the Catholics perceived ancient Rome as being subsumed into the universalism of the Roman Catholic Church. As such, this collection, the first of its kind, seeks to create a holistic overview of the distinctive cultural classical in Irish culture throughout the ages. What we learn is how deep articulations of migration through classical media have penetrated Ireland’s diasporic culture.
 The ebook editions of this book are available open access under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence on bloomsburycollections.com. Open access was funded by the European Research Council.
 https://bibliores.bloomsbury.com/getimage.aspx?bibliologin=1&s=50143b60-832b-4234-8b33-e73eaec8b4bb&cat=default&class=books&type=jpg&mode=&size=original&id=809450
 Ireland has an estimated diaspora of approximately 70 million people, ten times the actual population of the island, with a history of migration dating back to the medieval period. Why should we consider classical antiquity an important factor for understanding the intersection of migration and various Irish identities? This book proposes that ancient Greece and Rome lie at the root of a variety of Irish migration narratives and experiences, from our earliest written records until the twenty-first century, representing four central, and often interconnected, causes of migration: warfare; economics; education; religious grounds. Graeco-Roman models surface as expressions of participation and resistance, namely through an impetus to participate on the international stage and a vigorous resistance to exclusion.
 Participation manifests in knowledge transfer; in synchronistic narratives of Irish migratory origins; in defences of Irish civilization against claims of ‘barbarism’; in European debates on migratory and colonial policy; in cultural artistic exchange; in Irish-language translation; and in a networked literary diaspora. Resistance appears in rejection of disenfranchisement; in articulating the loss of dispossession and predicting restoration; in satirizing Anglo-Irish politics; in disrupting aesthetic expectations; in addressing the discrimination of exclusion as sectarian, xenophobic or gendered; in asserting the vigour of a minority language; in mining the power of pastoral; and in promoting hybridity and diversity over canonicity and hierarchy.
 The research presented in this book has been generously supported by the European Research Council (grant no. 818366).

abstract: This study examines the economic and sociocultural adaptation of Iranian migrants residing in Turkey by conceptualizing migration as a multidimensional and historically embedded social phenomenon. Migration has intensified since the post–Second World War era due to globalization, technological change, political instability, and economic inequalities, transforming it into a complex interaction between migrants and host societies. The study aims to identify key factors shaping migrants’ adaptation processes within this context. A quantitative correlational research design was employed. Data were collected from 392 Iranian migrants living in Turkey using a structured questionnaire that included the 21-item, five-dimensional SCAS-R scale and demographic variables. abstract: Background: Tuberculosis infection (TBI) has been identified as a driving factor for high tuberculosis (TB) prevalences globally. This study aims to systematically review outcomes from screening programs.<br><br>Methods: A systematic literature search was performed using PubMed and Embase including articles that contained data on TBI diagnosis or treatment completion from screening programs. Relevant data was extracted and processed through appropriate statistical analysis, estimating overall proportion of TBI screening results, offered treatment, treatment completion and further examining study characteristics through subgroup analysis. Risk of bias was assessed using the Critical Appraisal Checklist Programme and appraisal tools from The Joanna Briggs Institute. This study was registered with PROSPERO, CRD42024596568.<br><br>Findings: In 43 articles including 113 335 screened migrants the pooled proportion of migrants with a TBI diagnosis was 22% (95% CI 19-25; 23 445 of 113 335; I2=98%). Pooled analysis showed a significant decline in TBI proportions across decades and a significantly higher TBI proportion among migrants in WHO Western Pacific than WHO Europe. In 18 articles the pooled estimate of preventive treatment offered was 85% (95% CI 74-93; 7 792 of 10 693; I2=99%). In 28 articles the reported treatment completion rate among a total of 59 696 migrants was 77% (95% CI 71-83; 40 734 of 59 969; I2=98%). Pooled analysis showed a significantly higher completion percentage among migrants in WHO Europe than migrants in WHO Western Pacific.<br><br>Interpretation: The decline in TBI positive screening results is likely representative of a positive development in the eradication of TB with some remaining uncertainty based on the lacking alignment in screening programs, which skews the comparability and validity of the results. title: Immigration Flow Dependence and Demographic Debt: A Stylized Note on Delayed Adjustment after Immigration Restrictions
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: This note presents a stylized dynamic mechanism through which immigration restrictions may affect output even when their immediate impact appears modest. In the model, economic activity depends not only on the stock of migrants already present but also on the continuation of inflows, because new arrivals become residents, tenants, consumers, and job matches. With constant inflows, output follows a linear trend whose per-period increment is increasing in the inflow rate. A permanent cut in inflows has two effects: an immediate demand loss from forgone arrival expenditure and an accumulating shortfall in resident population relative to the pre-restriction path, which we call demographic debt. In the linear model, the economy moves onto a lower path with a smaller trend increment. If the cumulative resident shortfall exceeds available buffersvacancies, inventories, labor-market slack, and preserved organizational capacity-additional nonlinear losses can arise, making a delayed downturn possible. Expected reopening and the depreciation of migration-corridor capacity imply that temporary interruptions are less damaging than permanent restrictions and that recovery after a prolonged closure is asymmetric. The paper is a theoretical note. It does not claim causal identification for any historical episode, but it yields testable implications for timing, sectoral incidence, and recovery dynamics.

title: Immigration Militarization
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Immigration enforcement has undergone a generational shift from a civil law enforcement regime to a militarized mission. The past forty years has set a foundation of militarizing federal immigration agents, deploying troops at the border, and sending the armed forces overseas to curb migration to the United States. Recent efforts to deploy the National Guard to American cities, to use the Navy to kill alleged smugglers on the high seas, and to use special forces to decapitate foreign regimes represent escalations in a larger militarization pattern that seeks to signal America’s war on immigration on the world stage.<br><br>This article describes the multiple inflection points where military logics have taken control of immigration enforcement. From this descriptive analysis, the article further argues that this type of militarization presents a host of problems that have ripened in the past few years, including threats to democratic norms, beginning a new forever war, and newfound deprivations of liberty in a police state. Focusing on the militarization of immigration law learns from the lessons of previous domestic war policies to explore underappreciated links between executive power, corporate interests, nation-building, and social movements. This article concludes by considering using this new framework to explore dismantling most pernicious dangers of militarized immigration policy.

title: The NeuroLegal Method™: Closing the Credibility Gap in Immigration Law — Why Trauma-Informed Neurobiological Assessment Transforms Immigration Case Outcomes
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Immigration cases involving trauma survivors face a structurally embedded and systematically unaddressed crisis: the legal standards governing credibility assessment are incompatible with the neuroscience of trauma memory. Immigration adjudicators-bound by the REAL ID Act and heightened scrutiny protocols-evaluate credibility through a framework that presupposes chronological consistency, vivid factual recall, and narrative linearity. Neuroscience demonstrates, however, that traumatic experience is encoded in implicit, sensory, and fragmented memory systems that are constitutively nonlinear. The result is a system in which well-prepared cases are lost not on the merits, but on the misidentification of neurobiological trauma symptoms as evidentiary weakness. This white paper introduces the NeuroLegal Method™ (NLM)-a proprietary evaluation framework developed by Dr. Nilda Pérez, DSL, LCSW, at the NeuroLegal Institute™-as a systematic, reproducible solution to this gap. The NLM translates the neurobiological presentation of trauma into legally defensible, adjudicator-ready evidentiary documentation across asylum, VAWA, U visa, T visa, and removal defense matters. Drawing on research in trauma neuroscience, immigration law, and forensic evaluation methodology, this paper demonstrates why the NLM represents a structurally necessary advancement for the humanitarian immigration field-and why current evaluation models are insufficient to the task.

title: Resurrecting Immigration Releases
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: The nation's "mandatory" immigration-detention laws sustain its largest civil-imprisonment system-and just radically expanded in scope and breadth. These laws consign broad swaths of suspected noncitizens to no-bail pretrial detention, denying tens of thousands of people facing civil regulatory charges any chance to prove they need not be detained. These laws turn split-second arrest decisions into jail sentences. They force people to give up meritorious claims. And they confound the historic presumptions-liberty, innocence, prosecutorial discretion, and bail-that undergird other pretrial-detention regimes.&nbsp; <br><br>Although mandatory immigration detention conflicts with fundamental constraints on analogous detention regimes, the Supreme Court has treated it as exceptional and distinct. On this account, pretrial detention-detention pending proceedings to determine if a person is deportable-has been a "constitutionally valid aspect" of the deportation process for "more than a century" and was well accepted from a constitutional standpoint before any opportunity for release came along. Yet jurisprudence invoking this narrative tells us almost nothing about how detention actually operated at the time and, consequently, what type of detention or process early history and precedent may have enshrined. This Article takes on that task. It draws on critical sources of administrative law-early agency rules, binding interpretations, policy, and case files mined from the archives-to recover the lost history of pretrial-detention power and process during the deportation system's founding and formative years. This examination reveals that, in fact, the opportunity for release was virtually always part of deportation's early pretrial-detention scheme; any pretrial detention deemed constitutionally valid during that period came with the possibility of release. And it offers insight on why, showing that the agency's power to release was understood to be critical for a constitutionally permissible regime. Ultimately, this Article illuminates aspects of the early pretrial system that bear on pressing questions about detention and release in the contemporary scheme, and, as mandatory detention hurtles toward massive expansion, provides historical support for arguments to resurrect release.

title: <p>When Judges Become Asylum Seekers: Judicial Independence, Systemic Pressure and International Refugee Protection</p>
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Judicial independence is a foundational principle of the rule of law and democratic governance. Yet in a number of legal systems the formal guarantees of judicial autonomy coexist with informal mechanisms of executive control that progressively erode the impartiality of justice. This article examines the development and operation of such mechanisms in the Russian Federation, drawing on the author's professional experience as a federal judge and court president in Russia between 2008 and 2019.&nbsp; <div> The article analyses how executive pressure, the manipulation of performance metrics, and the expectation that judges should themselves 'guess' the required outcome created structural conditions in which judicial independence became not merely constrained but, in substance, fictitious. Drawing on the author's first-hand experience, the article traces how the Russian judiciary was gradually brought under the control of the Federal Security Service (FSB) and other organs of the executive, and contributes to the literature on authoritarian legalism and the instrumentalisation of law.&nbsp; </div> <div> The article further shows that the capture of the judiciary confronts a conscientious judge with a choice: to participate in the destruction of justice, or to refuse-and thereby become a target of persecution in turn. A judge who refuses to accept and participate in the new configuration of power finds himself exposed to the threat of fabricated criminal prosecution and compelled to seek protection abroad. Through his own case, the author argues that such a situation is a particular, and insufficiently examined, application of the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol: persecution for refusing to participate in the unlawful exercise of state power may constitute a ground for protection on the basis of political opinion or membership of a particular social group. </div>

title: Federal Broadband Investment and Rural Business Formation: Evidence from Rejected Applicants
reasons: no migration vocabulary; no Ireland reference
abstract: Most evaluations of federal broadband subsidies compare funded places to eligible places that never sought the money. I instead compare them to places that wanted the money and were denied: rural counties that applied for the same funds and lost. To draw that comparison I hand-build a universe of 328 such counties, whose applications to the $7.2 billion Broadband Initiatives Program and Broadband Technology Opportunities Program under the 2009 Recovery Act were all rejected, a roster of denied demand absent from any public file. This comparison holds demand for public broadband investment fixed and isolates what the funding itself did. Funded counties ended up with about 0.8 percent more business establishments than rejected applicants, on the order of 51,000 additional business locations. That magnitude survives the tighter comparison, corroborating earlier work rather than overturning it. The comparison matters because the standard eligible, unfunded control is itself 47 percent rejected applicants, since eligibility records who could apply, not who did. That share is the program’s rejection rate among eligible applicants, so eligibility-based estimates are not comparable across programs. This matters most for the $42 billion BEAD rollout, whose competitive subgrants already record who applied and who was rejected, exactly what a cleaner evaluation needs.

title: Hiring Discrimination Against Transgender Job Applicants in the US Labor Market

abstract: We investigate the extent of hiring discrimination against transgender individuals across the United States and how it varies by transgender identity, race, and geography. Through a correspondence study with more than 5,600 applications to entry-level positions, we find that transgender individuals are 2.1 percentage points (15%) less likely to get a callback. However, this aggregate effect masks important heterogeneity: callback penalties for transgender women and non-binary applicants are substantially larger in historically Republican-leaning labor markets, at 4.4–5.8pp relative to cisgender men. While Black applicants have lower callback rates overall, we do not find evidence that discrimination by transgender identity differs by race. We do not find evidence that the recent introduction or passage of anti-transgender legislation is associated with greater discrimination against transgender applicants. These results highlight that underlying political climates are more strongly associated with employer discrimination toward transgender applicants than increased salience due to anti-transgender legislation.

abstract: This article evaluates Ireland's strategy for positioning itself as a Eurozone headquarters for Islamic finance, in the context of the country's broader efforts to attract foreign direct investment following the 2008 financial crisis and subsequent EU-IMF bailout programme. Part C offers policy recommendations, including a comprehensive review of Ireland's tax regime modeled on comparable reviews conducted in the UK, Australia, and Hong Kong; stronger institutional networking with Gulf state financial authorities; public awareness campaigns targeting market participants; and increased investment in academic research on Islamic finance at Irish universities. The article concludes that while Ireland has taken meaningful first steps, more decisive government action is required to realize its ambition of becoming a genuine gateway for Middle Eastern investment into the Eurozone.

title: Preparing for the Next Round of New gTLDs: Governance and Resilience Lessons for Applicants

abstract: As the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) prepares to launch a second round of new generic Top-Level Domain (gTLD) applications, applicant preparedness is often framed in narrow technical and financial terms. This paper argues that such an approach is increasingly insufficient. Drawing on governance precedents, objection dynamics, and institutional patterns emerging from the first application round, it identifies non-technical risks that have proven decisive in application outcomes. The analysis introduces three practical frameworks-the Adversary Map, the Precedent Map, and the Resilience Map-to help future applicants assess political exposure, procedural vulnerability, and long-term institutional endurance. It further contends that new gTLD applications should be understood not as short-term compliance exercises, but as multi-year governance engagements requiring sustained executive alignment, legal resilience, and strategic diplomacy. title: Did Federal Broadband Stimulus Improve Rural Health? A Comprehensive Bounding Analysis of Rejected ARRA Applicants

abstract: Federal broadband programs are promoted partly on rural-health grounds, yet credibly identified evidence on whether broadband improves rural health is scarce, and the $42 billion BEAD program makes the question pressing. This study estimates the short-run association between the 2009 federal broadband stimulus (the USDA Broadband Initiatives Program and the NTIA Broadband Technology Opportunities Program) and a battery of rural health and socioeconomic outcomes. A rejected-applicant differencein-differences design compares 2,448 funded counties to 263 trajectory-matched rejected applicants, contrasting the pre-award (2010-2013) and pre-COVID post-award (2018-2019) periods. I estimate effects on nineteen County Health Rankings outcomes spanning healthcare access, screening, health behaviors, mortality, mental health, and socioeconomic status, with cluster-robust, randomization-inference, family-wise falsediscovery-rate, and state-by-year fixed-effects checks. The award raised fiber availability by 2.8 percentage points relative to rejected applicants, yet I find no robust effect on any of the nineteen outcomes. The two conventionally significant baseline estimates (preventable hospitalizations and high-school graduation) are absorbed by state-byyear fixed effects, consistent with state-level confounding, though that specification may also absorb state-level treatment variation; child poverty survives that test but not a multiple-testing correction, and the rest are precise nulls with reported minimum detectable effects. The stimulus raised fiber availability only modestly, and that expansion produced no detectable short-run improvements in rural health or socioeconomic outcomes. The estimates bound the short-run health returns to a 2.8-percentage-point fiber increase below policy-relevant magnitudes, an input to the cost-benefit case for the far larger BEAD program.

abstract: A policy-induced rural broadband expansion lowered adolescent fertility, and the response appears to operate through the information and opportunity set rather than through new clinical capacity. This information-andopportunity-set margin, rather than the clinical service itself, distinguishes the result from the direct family-planning-access interventions in the literature. The estimate is robust to permutation inference, a staggered-adoption difference-indifferences estimator, and dropping any single state, and remains negative under partial-identification pre-trend bounds, surviving moderate deviations from parallel trends.

abstract: This article presents an analysis of a file concerning the racial assessment and contestation of a denaturalisation proceeding held in the Demorazza collection at the Central State Archive in Rome. The file relates to the naturalisation and subsequent denaturalisation of Giuseppe Blinderman, a ‘stateless' individual of Jewish origin (first formerly Russian and then formerly Italian) in Fascist Italy. Focusing on Blinderman's actions and skills in shaping his public identity according to the authorities' criteria, the article aims to reconstruct Fascist denaturalisation policies and assess the relationship between the event triggered by the anti-Semitic denaturalisation measure and the previous naturalisation process. As with most cases of denaturalisation due to anti-Semitic legislation, the latter also occurred under the Fascist regime, but before the turning point of 1936–38. Adopting a bottom-up perspective, the article thus raises questions about the continuities and discontinuities represented by Fascism and, particularly, with regard to Fascist anti-Semitic policies on citizenship, revealing the interplay between ‘race' and ‘nativeness'.

title: A very Valuable Citizenship? European Values and Citizenship after Commission v Malta
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: On 29 April 2025, the Court delivered its much-awaited ruling in the so called ‘Golden Passport’ case (Case C-181/23 <i>Commission v Malta</i>). The issue related to a ‘citizenship for investment’ scheme that Malta had operated for some years; pursuant to the scheme, Maltese citizenship could be obtained relatively quickly upon meeting certain financial requirements. The case was of crucial constitutional importance since, on the one hand, it was widely assumed that the conferral of nationality (unlike the withdrawal of nationality) fell within the exclusive competence of the Member States, as also provided for in Declaration No. 2, annexed to the Treaty of Maastricht. On the other hand, it is obvious that the attractiveness of the scheme was primarily due to the value of Union citizen ship– in terms of both internal free movement and external visa-free travel possibilities. The Court found the scheme to be incompatible with EU law, basing its reasoning primarily on the principle of solidarity, sincere cooperation and further constitutionalization of Article 2 TEU. There is no doubt that <i>Commission v Malta</i> is set to become a landmark case on the European constitutional landscape– not only in relation to the way we conceptualize citizenship, but also in the way we construe the Treaty foundational&nbsp;provisions more broadly. This annotation proceeds as follows: after summarizing the facts and parties’ submissions (Section 2), the Opinion (Section 3) and the judgment (Section 4), the annotation focuses on some of the more interesting issues arising from the case. In particular, following from some preliminary remarks (Section 5.1), the annotation explores how the ruling redefines the boundaries of Union citizenship (Section 5.2); the standard of review required and the applicability of the general principles (Section 5.3); the relationship with existing case law (Section 5.4); and the ‘bedrock’ of the bond of nationality, solidarity and values (Section 5.5). The annotation concludes by urging all EU institutions to concur in ensuring that the Union’s values are defended from external and internal threats alike.

title: Selecting for ‘the Right Places’: Racial Capitalism and Strategic Essentialism in Football Academies in West-Africa
reasons: no migration vocabulary; no Ireland reference
abstract: Sport has long been shaped by the narratives of natural group qualities and competencies, which is a central framework of racial capitalism. Different ethnic and racial groups are ascribed certain natural qualities which supposedly make them more or less equipped for sport or for given roles in sport. This presumption of deservedness has shaped the opportunities and nature of participation of groups. Black Africans often find their abilities reduced to a limited set of physical capabilities and their role largely concentrated in the positions where these skills are of high importance, while having limited opportunities in the other positions. As a result, they may adopt a strategic form of essentialism to increase their chances of selection. This paper examines how football academies in West Africa play the game of strategic essentialism in their effort to extract value from the global talent export market shaped by racial capitalism.

title: European Citizenship and Socio-Economic Integration -Beyond EU Citizenship and Social Protection
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: <div> As part of an edited collection on the added value of EU citizenship, this paper addresses the role of social citizenship. It argues that it is necessary to combine social rights as the third pillar of the Marshall trilogy with the integration paradigm characterising the European Union in general. This presupposes that European Social Citizenship is neither unaffordable luxury nor outdated in a Union threatened by external pressure and internal challenges.&nbsp; </div> <div> <br> </div> <div> When the EU stumbled from the global financial crisis of 2010 into the alleged migration crisis of 2015, just after Russia’s first invasion into Ukraine in 2014, the EU’s global role seemed more important than considerations for improving the lives of its people internally. Thus, it was perhaps no coincidence that the Court of Justice reversed decades of jurisprudence enhancing social protection for EU citizens on the move in 2014 with its Dano ruling (C-333/13 EU:C:2014:2358). Yet, there were and are countervailing developments. Politically, the reign of the Juncker Commission (2014-2019) reignited legislation in favour of social Europe following the adoption of the European Pillar of Social Rights in 2017, and the first van-der-Leyen Commission (2019-2024) did not openly reverse that trend. The second van-der-Leyen Commission steers a contradictory course between dismantling the concept of social sustainability and adding a housing policy to the EU Commission portfolio. The European Court of Justice has softened some of the harder edges of the doctrine. In the meantime, the global pandemic underlined the necessity of supranational resource pooling. It also should have revived social policy locally, nationally and transnationally. Accordingly, adding a serious European dimension to welfare systems to enhance their resilience to such threats is a timely task.&nbsp; </div> <div> <br> </div> <div> This should be a good time to reconsider the value of European social citizenship more broadly, as well as the contribution of EU citizenship as a rights-based concept. European Union social citizenship would exist if social rights were not only granted by nation states, but also by the European Union itself. So far, EU law and policy have been more successful in protecting those who move between Member States, than the majority of EU citizens who do not move from one Member State to the next, except perhaps for visits and holidays.&nbsp; </div> <div> <br> </div> <div> The chapter analyses threats to European social citizenship as well as developing ways forward suitable for an age of transnationalization of society and increasing global insecurities. It concludes that European social citizenship remains a contradictory and unsatisfactory construct. Even protection for free movers remains incomplete. However, the more important challenge is to address the perception that the EU gives little to the vast majority of its citizens not actively using free movement rights other than for leisure purposes. A return to a programme of EU harmonisation of labour rights, as well as steps towards social security rights beyond the free movement programmes could address these concerns.&nbsp; </div>

title: State Capacity Without Self-Provision: Separating Political Authority from Capability Provision in Small States
reasons: no migration vocabulary; no Ireland reference
abstract: <p>Small states are commonly analyzed through a capacity problem: they face high fixed costs, thin administrative pools, and vulnerabilities that make it difficult to reproduce the institutional apparatus of larger states. Yet this framing can obscure an important distinction between possessing a capability, directly providing it, and retaining political authority over the arrangements through which it is obtained.</p> <p>This paper develops a provision-authority separation framework for small-state capacity. It argues that a state can access monetary, customs, administrative, security, or other capabilities through durable external arrangements without thereby transferring all political authority over the relevant policy domain.</p> <p>Liechtenstein provides a structured case because its statehood combines extensive external provision with continued international sovereignty and demonstrable instances of policy divergence from its principal partner, Switzerland. The paper distinguishes three analytical questions: whether a capability is reliably accessible, who supplies or administers it, and where politically meaningful authority remains. It introduces the concepts of provision-authority separation and externalized state capacity, together with a qualitative capability-architecture test.</p> <p>The contribution is integrative rather than a claim that dependence, delegation, or external shelter are new phenomena. The central claim is that state capacity and state self-provision are not the same thing: the institutional location of a capability does not by itself determine where political authority resides.</p>

title: Rethinking Public Goods Provision: State and Non-State Security Provision in Displacement Settings
reasons: no migration vocabulary; no Ireland reference
abstract: In contexts of limited state capacity, how do state and non-state actors provide public goods to their communities? Existing research has identified “complementarity” and “substitution” as the two core logics that characterize the co-existence of state and non-state actors in service provision. We build on these logics by arguing that it is the level of aggregation of a public good that determines whether complementarity or substitution occurs. To test our argument, we focus on one specific domain: public security and protection. Leveraging multiple rounds of the UNIOM’s Site Assessment surveys of IDP camps in Nigeria, we find suggestive evidence of this hierarchical logic. State security forces appear to respond primarily when camps face threats directly related to armed conflict, such as attacks by Boko Haram, whereas non-state actors assume protective roles in response to community-level insecurities. However, neither state nor communal actors seem to increase security provision following more private and less urgent forms of insecurity, such as petty theft or domestic violence. This paper contributes to the literature on public goods provision, non-state governance, and state capacity by introducing a new way of understanding state-non-state interactions in public goods provision that moves beyond the Weberian paradigm.

title: Insurance Provision and Securitization Dynamics
reasons: no migration vocabulary; no Ireland reference
abstract: I provide a dynamic model of securitization (pooling and tranching of risky loans) where specialized intermediaries hold the junior tranches to create safe assets. To price different tranches, intermediaries can estimate the default correlation structure more precisely when more loans are securitized. The equilibrium features a self-reinforcing effect between high risk perceptions and low securitization. High risk perceptions reduce intermediaries' willingness to hold junior tranches, leading to low levels of securitization. Since low securitization reduces intermediaries' ability to learn, risk perception remains high, resulting in very slow recovery. The paper provides an potential explanation on the stagnant recovery of private-label residential mortgage-backed securities (PLS) market. During the financial crisis, the massive write-downs of subprime mortgage related securities not only wiped out intermediaries' capital, leading to the collapse of issuance in all major securitization markets but also sharply increased risk perception in PLS market. The higher risk perceptions in PLS market have kept issuance low until now while other securitization markets recovered after intermediaries' recapitalization.

abstract: <p>This report presents new evidence on sexual corruption - the abuse of public power for sexual gain - in the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. Here, sexual corruption refers to situations in which a public official implies, either openly or suggestively, that a public service or benefit will be granted in exchange for sexual favours. The report draws on original survey research designed by the DCU Anti-Corruption Research Centre (ARC) in collaboration with Transparency International (TI) Ireland and the Transparency Legal Advice Centre and funded by Research Ireland under the New Foundations scheme.</p> <p>The findings indicate that sexual corruption is present across a range of public service settings in both jurisdictions. Among respondents who answered the sexual corruption questions in the survey, <b>10.9% in the Republic of Ireland and 7.1% in Northern Ireland reported that they or someone they knew had encountered sexual corruption</b> in at least one public service domain. Even under a conservative assumption that all respondents who opted out of the sensitive module had encountered no such corruption, estimated prevalence remains higher in the Republic of Ireland (8.5%) than in Northern Ireland (6.6%).</p> <p>These findings are consistent with earlier evidence pointing to the <b>risk of</b> <b>sexual corruption </b>in Ireland, though the estimates are not directly comparable. TI’s 2021 Global Corruption Barometer (GCB), which found that 4% of the Irish respondents reported direct experience or knowledge of sexual corruption with 68% believing that it was likely to be a problem. Our survey asked about specific areas of interaction with public services, which may help to explain the higher reported incidence observed here by prompting respondents to think about specific public service settings and concrete experiences, rather than asking only for a general assessment of the issue.</p> <p>Reported experience spans multiple domains of public administration. In the Republic of Ireland, the highest reported prevalence is in policing, schools and universities, and immigration or passport services. In Northern Ireland, the highest reported prevalence is in schools and universities, policing, and local government. <b>Education and policing therefore emerge as particularly important areas of concern in both jurisdictions</b>.</p> <p>Taken together, the evidence suggests that sexual corruption is not an isolated or purely anecdotal phenomenon. Rather, it affects a meaningful minority of adults across both jurisdictions and warrants sustained institutional attention, effective reporting pathways, and stronger safeguards across vulnerable public service domains.</p>

title: Protection of Refugees in Africa Through IHL
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Africa plays a dual role in the refugee landscape: as both a source of cross-border displacement and a sanctuary for those fleeing persecution and armed conflict. To uphold refugee rights, nations have embraced the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol, while also pioneering the 1969 African Refugee Convention. Though this regional framework broadens the definition of refugees, it falls short in addressing the unique vulnerabilities refugees face in armed conflict situations. Instead of amending the convention, fragmented regional instruments under International Humanitarian Law (IHL) have been introduced to fill these gaps. Despite these efforts, the absence of robust scholarly discourse on the role and relevance of these IHL instruments in protecting refugees during armed conflicts has hampered progress. This article offers a critical and comprehensive analysis of Africa's scattered IHL instruments, underscoring their potential for improving refugee protection. It exposes a glaring deficiency: the lack of a regional court with jurisdiction over war crimes committed against refugees, which has allowed perpetrators to evade justice and left refugees without recourse. The article calls for urgent action. African Union member states must either ratify the long-pending Malabo Protocol to establish a continental criminal court or fully cooperate with the International Criminal Court (ICC). Without these measures, impunity will persist, and the promise of justice for refugees will remain elusive. This analysis underscores the imperative for a unified, enforceable justice mechanism to ensure accountability, uphold refugee rights, and protect the dignity of those displaced by conflict.

abstract: While Deafness can function as a cultural–linguistic identity with its own language and community norms, Deaf individuals may belong simultaneously to other social groups while sharing a Deaf identity. Throughout this work, Belenyi and Flora interpret Deafness and ethnicity through the lens of Social Identity Theory (SIT), which posits that individuals derive part of their self-concept from membership in social groups and predicts that group memberships shape self-concept and self-esteem. While SIT has its limitations, newer adaptations, such as self-categorization theory and identity process theory, allow for more nuanced interpretations. With a focus on Hungarian ethnic-minority Deaf people in Romania—and their partners and communities—the authors examine these insights to understand how Deaf people in Romania balance their ethnic and Deaf identities. Deaf people in East-Central Europe, especially in the multi-ethnic context of Romania, inhabit overlapping minority worlds. Although nation-building policies often emphasize linguistic and ethnic homogeneity, in practice Hungarian–Romanian relations within Deaf families and communities can reveal unexpected cultural bridges. This book combines a theoretical synthesis of Deaf identity, culture, and ethnicity with empirical life-course research to shed new light on how Deaf and ethnic identities intersect.

title: <p>The Enforcement Gap: Why Pakistan's Constitutional Anti-Discrimination Provisions Fail Ethnic Minorities in Practice</p>
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Pakistan's constitutional framework contains extensive textual commitments to equality and nondiscrimination. Articles 4, 25, 26 and 27 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1973 collectively promise equal treatment before the law, prohibit discrimination on grounds of race, religion, caste, sex and place of birth, and guarantee equal access to public places and state employment. Yet ethnic minorities in Pakistan, including the Baloch, Hazara, Pashtun and Sindhi communities, continue to face persistent and documented discrimination in employment, healthcare, education and access to justice. This article argues that the primary failure is not textual but institutional. Pakistan does not have a discrimination law problem in the conventional sense. What it has is a discrimination enforcement problem. Drawing on constitutional analysis, judicial decisions including the landmark Supreme Court judgment in Suo Moto Case No. 1 of 2014, the 2014 Jillani judgment on minority rights, and the Islamabad High Court ruling in Writ Petition No. 3719 of 2015, this article examines the structural gap between constitutional promise and practical reality. It identifies four interconnected causes of this gap: weak enforcement architecture, limited access to courts for marginalised communities, social and cultural attitudes that undermine formal legal protections, and the absence of a dedicated antidiscrimination statute. The article concludes with a framework of targeted reforms, including the case for a standalone anti-discrimination law and the emerging role of technology-assisted legal mechanisms in bridging the enforcement gap in developing economies.

abstract: This paper examines the influence of Zimbabwean permits on Zimbabwean migrants’ access to decent work in South Africa. While existing scholarship on migrant labour and decent work has largely focused on undocumented migrants, and studies on Zimbabwean permits have centred on their hidden policy aims and administrative experiences, little attention has been paid to how such permits shape labour outcomes. Drawing on Harvey’s notions of the logic of territory and the logic of capital, the paper analyses migrants’ experiences with work permits and their implications for decent work. The study is based on in-depth interviews with Zimbabwean migrant workers holding Zimbabwean permits. The findings reveal that although permits improve access to employment, they do not guarantee decent work. Instead, migrants remain concentrated in precarious forms of employment characterised by low wages, long hours and limited protection. The paper argues that the temporary nature of the permit regime produces a regulated and docile workforce, structurally embedded in precarious labour markets.

abstract: From the macro perspective of social equity and sustainable economic development, exploring the employment quality of returning rural migrant workers is an important approach to addressing the global issue of income inequality. Drawing on survey data of returning rural migrant workers in China, this study investigates the impact of social support on their employment quality and examines the underlying mechanism. The results show that social support significantly improves the employment quality of returning rural migrant workers. Mechanism analysis reveals that social support promotes the improvement of their employment quality by enhancing skill matching. Further heterogeneity analysis indicates that the promoting effect of social support is more pronounced among passively returning rural migrant workers, while the effect is weakened for those in characteristic protected villages; compared with the central region, social support exerts a stronger promoting effect on returning rural migrant workers in the eastern and western regions. title: A Universal Systems Framework for Understanding Discrimination: Application to Antisemitism, Racism, Religious Conflict, and Political Extremism

abstract: This paper presents a formalized Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF) for analyzing persistent forms of human discrimination, including antisemitism, racism, religious conflict, and political extremism. Grounded in four proposed universal laws-(1) the Law of System Integrity (Karma), (2) the Universal Law of Balance, (3) the Universal Feedback Loop Mechanism, and (4) the Universal Interconnected Nodes-the framework offers both a conceptual and mathematical apparatus for diagnosing systemic societal failure. We demonstrate that large-scale discrimination and conflict emerge not from isolated individual pathologies but from identifiable structural dynamics: defective belief propagation, equilibrium breakdown, runaway reinforcing feedback, and network-level amplification. A formal dynamical model is developed, stability conditions are derived via Lyapunov analysis, and case studies are applied across four historical and contemporary domains. The framework contributes a transdisciplinary diagnostic lens with implications for conflict prevention, governance, and social policy.

abstract: Climate change is a contributing factor to the high burden of infectious and noncommunicable diseases in Africa, in particular a resource-poor setting already faced with worsening humanitarian and socio-economic crises, as well as a rising incidence and prevalence of noncommunicable and chronic diseases. Thus, examining studies on the triad, climate change–migration–health, would provide more direction on how climate change mitigation can be incorporated into health system planning in Africa. This paper seeks to review studies on the climate change–migration–health triad with a particular focus on those that address elderly health outcomes in relation to the triad and provide guidelines on how governments can enhance their health systems and mitigate climate change to enable the elderly and elderly migrants to cope and age healthily. The author conducted a review of research articles, reviews, and documents using online databases, including Google Scholar, Google, and Web of Science. The following keywords were combined with the Boolean operators AND and OR to conduct the search: ageing population, environmental changes, climate change, gerontology, and the elderly. Limiters were: language: papers published in English on the themes; and period: papers and documents from 1990 to 2025. Documents, papers, and articles were from both regional (African region) and international sources. The author’s search lasted 3 weeks and yielded 44 articles, of which 18 were selected for thematic analysis. Thematic analysis of articles revealed that climate change impacts on the elderly are severe, with the elderly migrants presenting a greater vulnerability; impacts of climate change on African health systems are projected to be severe due to weak health systems. This paper underscores the need for African health systems to integrate data-driven climate change mitigation strategies into health systems and improve community engagement and international collaboration to tackle climate change and health system challenges.

abstract: The remaining extant manuscripts of ancient Irish poetry show how from the beginning the Irish people identified and defined themselves and their experiences in terms of their surroundings, namely Ireland as a fertile land surrounded by the sea. They also attest to the richness of Irish vernacular literature at a time when much of Western Europe had adopted Latin for such purposes. These manuscripts survived in Continental compilations and were subjected to the scrutiny of late 19th and early 20th-century scholars. The Irish revival of the second half of the Victorian era coincided with calamities such as the Great Famine, heightening friction between Catholics and Protestants, and an immense wave of immigration to North America. Irish nationalism had been gaining momentum for some time, and was clearly manifested after the 1850s in the writings of many Irish figures that sought to reclaim their country along with its cultural heritage. The return to myth and legend was one step in the right direction, and the writers and translators of the time explored the endless ways to highlight the richness of their past by making it available to contemporary and future readers. Such literature aimed to engage the reader as well as assert the Irish character in the face of the British monolith, and it also had a considerable impact on the Irish struggle for independence. This research addresses such sentiments in the mythology-centred writings and translations of Jane Francesca Agnes, Lady Wilde; Kuno Meyer and William Butler Yeats.

abstract: ABSTRACT This contribution examines the affects circulating in Rosaleen McDonagh’s auto/biographical narrative of her girlhood and youth, Unsettled (2021). It focuses especially on shame, rage, self-love and pride, and the relationships and alliances they hinder or help to build among vulnerable collectives in Ireland. McDonagh’s text constitutes a brave public act of denouncement and political empowerment, bringing to the public scene a number of crimes of hate against vulnerable collectives that mainstream Irish culture would rather wish silenced. Her writing serves as archival record of systemic and systematic abuse on extraordinary bodies, such as Irish Travellers, disabled children and adults, racialised migrants, girls and women, and queer persons. I sustain that this public denouncement provides a good example of feminist killjoy activism in that it critically exposes structural abuses on those collectives while simultaneously working to reinforce political networks and communities of care. abstract: Abstract Homelessness remains a critical social issue in Ireland, yet its true scale is systematically obscured by definitional limitations, methodological inconsistencies, and political interference in data collection. While official statistics reported 16,058 individuals relying on emergency accommodation as of July 2025 (a rise of +244% since July 2015), this figure excludes substantial populations: rough sleepers, domestic violence survivors, asylum seekers, and those experiencing hidden homelessness through enforced parental co-residence. This article examines the politics of homelessness enumeration through a critical analysis of seven data sources, policy documents spanning 2014–2025 and stakeholder interviews. The study reveals how Ireland’s measurement system exemplifies the political life of numbers. The analysis exposes five interconnected dimensions of measurement failure: fragmentation of sources and measurement approaches, methodological inconsistencies that undermine longitudinal analysis, systematic undercounting that renders substantial populations invisible, documented political manipulation and data integrity concerns, and structural barriers that impede comprehensive data collection and analysis. The findings demonstrate how apparently technical decisions about data collection and analysis become sites of political contestation. The research reveals the measurement politics in contemporary welfare states, demonstrating the need for inclusive frameworks, integrated systems, and transparent practices that prioritize social justice over administrative convenience.

abstract: The value of a reproductive justice framework within an Irish context was recently highlighted in a special issue of the journal Éire-Ireland, “Women’s Health and Reproductive Justice in Ireland” (2021). In their introduction the editors describe how their experience of living and working in the United States has influenced their understanding of the material conditions of abortion access in Ireland and its links to histories of healthcare, institutional racism and the treatment of migrants. In this essay I shift the transnational gaze southwards, to consider how the terrain of Latin American feminist materialism – a vibrant and influential space of feminist activism and theory – can help elucidate the excavatory practices of contemporary Irish women writers and artists responding to Ireland’s histories of reproductive oppression. More precisely, I explore how the cultural critique of the Mexican writer Cristina Rivera Garza can theoretically inform a reading of Irish materialist poetics in the wake of Mother and Baby Homes and Magdalene Laundries. In so bridging the distance between Rivera Garza’s writing and the work of artists and poets in Ireland, this essay seeks to further internationalist understanding of the cultural dimensions for struggles for reproductive justice.

abstract: ABSTRACT This article analyses the representation of the relational ethics of alterity in Kevin Curran’s novel Youth (2023) to show how recent Irish fiction addresses the plight of the young Black Irish in contemporary Ireland. Drawing on the ethics of alterity and relational ethics, this analysis examines Curran’s representation of the young Irish “Other” with two second-generation immigrant teenagers, Angel and Princess, black and born in Ireland of immigrant parents and desperate to belong to society. As the victims of economic precarity and racism, these youngsters constitute the faces of alterity of the Black Irish “Other” who, during their growing processes, depend on the relational ethics of empathy and solidarity and face whiteness and Irishness as exclusionary. The analysis shows that Curran’s representation of these youngsters situates ethics within the discourse of relationships within the community characterised by interdependency, support, and acceptance and recognises the alterity of the Black Irish as a factor which characterises their experiences. The novel represents both the lack of acceptance and the embrace of the “young other” and situates positive transformation within the realm of individual relationships. This article proves that Kevin Curran’s Youth advocates the importance of relational nodes which promote ethical solutions to alterity.

abstract: ABSTRACT David Wheatley’s Child Ballad (2023) bears witness to the mutual vulnerabilities of his family and the environment, demonstrating a relational ontology between them. With a sense of urgency and importance, communicated by its focus on the vulnerable child, the collection depicts a migratory model of habitation across the archipelago of Ireland and Scotland. title: Eugenio Pacelli and the Vatican’s Irish Plan to Save Baptized Jews (1938–1939)
reasons: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Shortly after the enactment in September 1938 of the first of Fascist Italy’s anti-Jewish ‘racial laws’, which mandated the expulsion from the country of all foreign Jews, desperate pleas for help began flooding into the Vatican. The pleas came overwhelmingly from Jews who had been baptised. Vatican secretary of state, Eugenio Pacelli, initially saw in Ireland the best possibility for a solution. Over the next months a thick correspondence developed between Pacelli and the nuncio in Dublin, Paschal Robinson. The nuncio in turn relied on Sir Joseph Glynn, president of Ireland’s St Vincent de Paul Society, to spearhead the resettlement effort. Not long after Pacelli became pope himself in March 1939, Vatican hopes for the Irish plan faded. Vatican ambitions for Ireland foundered on the lack of support among both the Church hierarchy and the general population for helping refugees regarded as Jews, notwithstanding their baptismal status.

title: From Marxism to Social Democracy: Evolving Leftist and Ethno-National Perspectives in the European Kurdish Komala Diaspora

abstract: Abstract: This article examines the ideological-political transformation of first-generation Kurdish political refugees from Iranian/Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhelat) with leftist political backgrounds, now residing in Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, and France. It explores how their ethno-national identity and leftist ideology, situated within the Kurdish diaspora, shape their political orientation in their host countries. The study is based on twenty-six in-depth interviews with current and former members of the offshoots of the Iranian Kurdistan Toilers’ Revolutionary Association ( Komalay Shoreshgeri Zahmatkeshani Kurdistani Eran, or Komala). Findings indicate that exposure to a European political-ideological atmosphere has shifted their stance from authoritarian to libertarian leftism, strengthening the role of Kurdish identity in their political attitude and orientation and fostering a balance between their ethnic and ideological affiliations. Beyond advocating for the Kurdish diaspora, their political engagement in Europe serves as a form of transnational lobbying to influence European countries’ politics regarding Kurdish rights in their country of origin.

title: Do Industrial Robots Lower Employment Quality for Manufacturing Migrant Workers in China?
authors: Qian Kang; Zhoufu Yan; Ali Sher
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: ABSTRACT China's 297.35 million migrant workers face the challenge of improving their livelihoods, maintaining social stability, and securing high‐quality employment. However, the impact of automation on the quality of their employment remains unclear, with concerns that automation may diminish employment quality for this group. This study utilizes data from the China Labor Dynamics Survey (CLDS) and applies robust statistical methods to assess the effect of industrial robots on the employment quality of migrant workers in China. The findings reveal a U‐shaped relationship between the use of industrial robots and employment quality. Initially, employment quality declines due to skill mismatches caused by automation, but this trend reverses as the labor market adjusts to technological advancements. Furthermore, the study examines sectoral and individual differences in employment quality during the era of robotization, highlighting the moderating effects of urban scale and the household registration system. To support migrant workers in transitioning to stable and rewarding employment in an automated economy, the government should prioritize skill development programs and ensure the equitable distribution of technological benefits.

title: The Squeezed Middle in Digital Financial Services: Ireland's Warning for European Consumer Protection Policy
authors: Marie-Laure Ryan; Huanhuan Xiong; F. Carton; J. B. McCarthy

abstract: Abstract      This paper examines how digital financial services affect consumer welfare across income distributions using Ireland as a critical case study for European consumer protection policy. Our analysis of 11,128 Irish households from the 2020 EU Survey on Income and Living Conditions reveals that technology shows no direct association with consumer welfare (β=0.0022, p=0.969). Instead, it operates only through mediating channels that frequently fail for middle-income consumers. We identify a "squeezed middle" phenomenon where households between the 20th and 70th income percentiles experience persistent financial strain despite technology access. Young adults remain in negative financial well-being through the 70th income percentile despite 96.2 per cent technology access, suggesting structural barriers that technology cannot address. Immigration status creates the largest technology gap at 40.7 per cent, yet technology fails to explain welfare disparities between immigrants and natives. These findings from Ireland, where fintech adoption rates reach 71 per cent compared to the European average of 64 per cent, challenge the European Union's €150 billion digital infrastructure investment introduced on automatic consumer benefits. We identify three mechanisms explaining this failure: capability mismatch where technological resources exceed user capabilities, economic constraints override where fundamental economic barriers overwhelm technology benefits, and satisfaction illusion where technology increases perceived control without improving objective outcomes. As Europe's most digitalised economy, Ireland provides an early warning for other member states pursuing similar strategies.   JEL Codes:   D14, D18, G51, I31

title: 'I felt like I just belonged': urban multiculture and black Irish migrants in post-war Britain.
reasons: MANUAL: post-war Irish migrants in Britain
institutions: School of History, Anthropology, Philosophy and Politics, Queen's University Belfast, 25 University Square, United Kingdom.
abstract: This article reevaluates historians' understanding of the Irish in post-war Britain from the perspective of a previously unresearched population, black and mixed-race Irish migrants. Writing on the Irish in Britain has lingered on themes such as stereotyping, discrimination, and ethnic profiling. More widely, some historians have framed Irish emigration and the diaspora around motifs of exile and reluctant departure, while others have highlighted the liberating potential of departure. Oral histories with black Irish migrants fall firmly into the latter, emancipatory camp, depicting urban, multicultural Britain as a site of acceptance and belonging. Far from presenting emigration as a reluctant withdrawal from a cherished homeland, Irish people of colour narrated their departure as a liberating exit from an upbringing of alienation and abuse. These findings have wider implications for understanding the dynamics of British multiculture. Black Irish narrators revelled in the anonymity granted by post-war British diversity, which allowed them to discover and embrace their blackness. Some found belonging within the black communities of urban Britain, especially London. Conversely, they faced rejection from Irish diasporic spaces, which were characterized by conservative, Catholic and exclusively white conceptions of Irishness. The article therefore uses previously unexplored narratives to reframe our understanding of the Irish community in Britain and the broader context of urban multiculture in which it existed.

title: Relative MYC downregulation and RUNX2 upregulation orchestrate partial epithelial‐mesenchymal transition in colorectal cancer tumor budding and poorly differentiated clusters
authors: Tsuyuha Koba; Takashi Hibiya; Takahiro Shibayama; Kenichiro Kato; H. Onizuka; Kashi Satomi; Kiyotaka Nagahama; Eiji Sunami; N. Abe; Eiryo Kawakami; Junji Shibahara; Akimasa Hayashi

abstract: Tumor budding and poorly differentiated clusters are key prognostic indicators in colorectal cancer, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying their formation remain incompletely characterized. Using the GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiler, we analyzed gene expression profiles across tubular components, transitional zones, and tumor budding and poorly differentiated cluster regions in 12 colorectal cancer cases. While histopathological assessment revealed no definitive evidence of complete epithelial‐mesenchymal transition in tumor budding or poorly differentiated clusters, transcriptional analysis demonstrated significant upregulation of epithelial‐mesenchymal transition‐related genes (ZEB1, ZEB2, SNAI2) alongside maintained epithelial marker expression, indicating a partial epithelial‐mesenchymal transition phenotype. Tumor budding and poorly differentiated cluster regions showed reduced proliferative activity with significant downregulation of MYC and its target genes involved in protein synthesis and cell cycle progression. Conversely, RUNX2 and its targets were significantly upregulated in tumor budding and poorly differentiated cluster regions, particularly genes mediating cell adhesion, migration, and extracellular matrix interactions. KRT80 showed striking upregulation in tumor budding and poorly differentiated cluster regions, correlating with RUNX2 expression. This reciprocal pattern of MYC downregulation and RUNX2 upregulation appears to contribute to maintaining the hybrid epithelial–mesenchymal state characteristic of tumor budding and poorly differentiated cluster regions. Our findings reveal that the formation of these regions involves transcriptional changes preceding morphological alterations, with RUNX2 potentially driving this invasive phenotype while preserving epithelial features. These insights may enhance our understanding of the mechanisms driving colorectal cancer progression and identify potential therapeutic targets for aggressive disease. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

abstract: This research aims to analyze the economic function of government in addressing market failures and the challenges of its implementation amidst the dynamics of the modern economy. Theoretically, the price mechanism acts as a signal to coordinate supply and demand, but in practice, markets often fail to produce efficiency and fairness simultaneously. Market failures arise from externalities (e.g., pollution), limited provision of public goods, information asymmetry, and imperfect competition such as monopolies and cartels. This research uses a descriptive qualitative method thru literature review and document analysis of books, journals, and policy reports. The findings indicate that state intervention is necessary to maintain economic stability and protect vulnerable groups, especially when externalities, information asymmetry, the unavailability of public goods, and non-competitive market structures (cartels/monopolies) cause distortions. Effective policies must be able to align economic actors' incentives with social goals thru the internalization of social costs, for example, with taxes, technical standards, emission limits, permits, and clean technology incentives. The government also plays a role in providing basic services and public goods thru direct provision, public-private partnerships, or targeted subsidies, accompanied by enhanced transparency and public literacy to reduce information inequality. Conceptually, this intervention aligns with the allocation, distribution, and stabilization functions, which demand data-driven diagnosis and measurable, adaptive, and accountable policy governance.

abstract: Abstract Since the 2008 financial crisis, the UK has emerged as a popular destination for young Spanish women navigating labour precariousness through (formerly intra-European Union) migration. Many adopt the au pair pathway as a strategic means to improve their English language skills and enhance future employability. However, while framed as a “cultural exchange”, the au pair scheme has faced sustained critique for masking a reality often characterised by precarious work, exploitation, and even abuse due to the great dependency of au pairs on host families and the various forms of worker control au pairs are exposed to. title: Materialising Digital Borderscapes: Examining the Effects of Digital Systems on Asylum Seekers and Refugees
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Digitalisation is increasingly adopted in the public sector in South Africa. The country’s Department of Home Affairs has a significant digitalisation project that aims to improve its efficiency in service delivery. Despite this project, it was the Covid‐19 pandemic that saw the introduction of a digital interface to manage the bureaucracy of asylum seeker and refugee administration. This article examines the impacts of this asylum seeker and refugee permit extension online system. The article traces how the online system works to refigure how asylum seekers access the state and the possibility of securing documentation. We demonstrate that this online system has effects far greater than simply improved efficiency; instead, it fundamentally refigures the borderscapes navigated by asylum seekers and refugees. Here, digitalisation shifts bureaucratic responsibility to the asylum seekers and refugees, and in so doing, distances them from the state. We show this by paying attention to how the online system changes the materialities of asylum seeking; the spaces in which protection is sought; as well as the practices thereof, where actors other than the state are called on for assistance. In the world of technological interventions, this online system for permit renewal is a seemingly mundane example of digitalisation; yet its effects on the possibilities for social, legal, and even economic inclusion of asylum seekers and refugees are significant.

title: Integration of Migrants from Ukraine into Polish Society: International Law, Challenges, and Opportunities

abstract: This research paper investigates wartime migration patterns of Ukrainian citizens in the initial period of the full-scale Russian invasion and examines the complex dynamics of migration and integration in Poland in the following years in the light of international and national law. The conflict triggered one of the largest refugee crises in Europe since World War II, with Poland emerging as the primary destination for displaced Ukrainians. The study analyzes the legal and social dimensions of this process, situating it within the framework of international law, international humanitarian law, and national legislation. It argues that Poland’s response represents a distinctive global phenomenon: a largely peaceful, inclusive, and effective approach to managing a sudden and massive influx of displaced persons. At the same time, the absence of a coherent long-term integration policy, combined with shifting public sentiment, generates both risks and opportunities for future social cohesion. The article advances an original theoretical contribution by introducing the concept of large-scale integration, a pioneering analytical framework in migration and legal scholarship. It defines this phenomenon as the rapid, law-based incorporation of an exceptionally large population of displaced persons into the structures of a modern state. This concept, developed here for the first time, provides a new lens through which to interpret the intersection of humanitarian response, international law, and domestic governance. Closely related is the notion of emergency integration, describing the legal and institutional mechanisms that enable swift adaptation of state systems during mass displacement. Methodologically, the study follows a doctrinal and comparative legal approach complemented by interpretive social analysis. It examines the interaction between international instruments (including the 1951 Geneva Convention and the EU Temporary Protection Directive), Polish special-purpose legislation, and the evolving public response. The findings reveal that Poland’s model combined legal innovation with civic solidarity, offering an instructive example of rights-based governance in the face of large-scale displacement. By reframing Poland’s experience as both a national and global phenomenon, the article contributes to migration, humanitarian, and international law scholarship. It proposes a new conceptual and normative framework for analyzing how law, policy, and social agency converge to enable large-scale, peaceful integration – a process that remains fragile yet potentially transformative for the future of global migration governance.

title: A Sociological Perspective on the Integration Process of Migrants in Western Europe: Focusing on Migrants from Third Countries

abstract: This article examines the process of migrant integration in Western Europe from a sociological perspective, with a specific focus on migrants from third countries. Integration is conceptualized as a complex, multidimensional, and bidirectional process shaped by interactions between migrants and host societies. Drawing on classical and contemporary sociological theories, including approaches to assimilation, multiculturalism, and transnationalism, the study highlights the relevance of structural, social, cultural, and political dimensions in shaping integration trajectories.The article adopts a qualitative methodology based on a systematic review of sociological literature, policy documents, and institutional reports produced by the OECD, the European Commission, and the International Organization for Migration. These sources are used to analyze key forms and indicators of integration, such as labor market participation, access to education and housing, social relations, cultural adaptation, and civic and political engagement, within the context of Western European integration policies.The analysis indicates that migrants from third countries face more substantial barriers to integration than native populations and intra-EU migrants. These challenges include legal and administrative constraints, labor market segmentation, overqualification, discrimination, limited social networks, and restricted opportunities for civic participation. The article concludes that effective integration requires comprehensive and inclusive policy approaches that address structural inequalities, promote social cohesion, and support mutual adaptation between migrants and host societies. This multidimensional sociological perspective contributes to ongoing academic debates and provides a foundation for future empirical research and evidence-based policymaking. abstract: Abstract The February 2022 escalation of the Russo-Ukrainian war sparked Europe's largest forced migration crisis since World War II, displacing over 6 million Ukrainians. Understanding the factors influencing entrepreneurial confidence among this population is essential for designing effective economic integration policies and support programmes. While social capital theory has dominated migrant entrepreneurship research for four decades, its relevance in contexts of forced displacement—characterised by disrupted networks, incomplete institutional knowledge, and high uncertainty—remains theoretically and empirically contested. This study tests five competing hypotheses about entrepreneurial confidence among Ukrainian migrant entrepreneurs in the UK, drawing from social capital, cognitive-perceptual, prospect theory, and cultural embeddedness frameworks. Using cross-sectional survey data collected between March and September 2025 (N = 245–312 across hypotheses), we measured entrepreneurial confidence as a composite index across four dimensions: opportunity identification, resource acquisition, regulatory navigation, and customer base development. Our findings reveal that perceived environmental favourability is the strongest predictor of entrepreneurial confidence, with entrepreneurs reporting favourable perceptions exhibiting substantially higher confidence than those with unfavourable views. Cultural embeddedness demonstrates significant effects when strategically deployed: entrepreneurs view cultural connections as critical, reporting markedly higher confidence than those who perceive them as merely helpful. Risk perception is significantly negatively associated with confidence. Contrary to four decades of social capital scholarship, professional network strength shows no meaningful association with entrepreneurial confidence—a null finding that persisted despite sufficient statistical power. These results fundamentally challenge the dominance of social capital theory in migrant entrepreneurship research, suggesting that cognitive-perceptual and cultural factors may be more salient predictors of entrepreneurial confidence in forced-migration contexts than traditional network-based explanations.

title: Improving the Educational and Training Opportunities of Adolescent Girls by Reducing Early Pregnancies in Kibaha District, Tanzania
