abstract:
AIM
This study examined service providers' perspectives on how race, ethnicity, and immigration status shape help-seeking experiences and institutional responses for Black, Latino, and immigrant male victims of female-perpetrated intimate partner violence (IPV).


METHOD
Semi-structured Zoom interviews were conducted with 10 service providers, primarily from the United States (with one provider each from Canada and Ireland), who work with male victims of female-perpetrated IPV. Participants included 5 attorneys, 2 domestic violence agency professionals, 2 mental health clinicians, and 1 executive director of a men and families center. Data were analyzed using an inductive reflexive thematic analytic approach.


RESULTS
Three themes were identified: (1) Barriers to Help-Seeking, Protection, and Support, reflecting intersecting internal, structural, immigration-related, and institutional constraints; (2) Identity-Responsive Practices, describing providers' strategies for adapting services to diverse male victims; and (3) Gender as the Initial Lens of Institutional Interpretation, reflecting providers' descriptions of gender as the initial lens through which male victimization was interpreted, with race, ethnicity, and immigration status shaping institutional responses.


CONCLUSION
From the perspective of service providers, improving protection for Black, Latino, and immigrant male victims of female-perpetrated IPV requires more than stigma reduction. Findings suggest that systems should address credibility bias, expand culturally and linguistically responsive services, and integrate immigration-informed pathways to promote more equitable access to safety.

abstract: Abstract This reflective essay interrogates the complex interplay between identity, memory and migration through personal narrative, historical analysis and cultural representation. It draws on the intersections of my own personal experiences with the academic research I have conducted, interrogating anew the concepts of memory, identity and collective ideas of belonging as manifested by the documents we are entitled to carry. Using the Netflix series Transatlantic as an entry point, it explores how identity documents – passports, permits and bureaucratic records – shape individual experiences and collective histories, particularly in contexts of displacement and state surveillance. I connect these depictions to my own migratory background, highlighting the privileges of dual citizenship and the inequalities embedded in what Schahar termed the ‘birthright lottery’. Drawing on archival research into Irish and British travel permit systems during the Second World War, the piece situates historical identity regimes within contemporary debates on datafication, statelessness and the governance of migration. It further reflects on the development of the History of Identity Documentation in European Nations (HIDDEN) research network (funded by Cooperation in Science and Technology [COST], CA21120), which examines the past, present and future of identity documentation. Ultimately, the essay argues for critical engagement with how identity is constructed, contested and experienced across time.

title: Citizen science reveals incipient naturalisation of non-native palms (Arecaceae) in South Africa
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract Palms (Arecaceae) are among the most widely cultivated plant families globally, yet their invasion ecology remains poorly understood outside a few well-studied tropical systems. South Africa has cultivated non-native palms for over a hundred years, but no palm species are currently listed as invasive in national legislation. We used iNaturalist data, supplemented with herbarium and arboretum records, to compile the first comprehensive inventory of non-native palms in South Africa, model habitat suitability, identify areas of high naturalisation susceptibility, and propose monitoring priorities. In total, 145 non-native palm taxa were recorded in the country. From 4,220 quality-filtered iNaturalist records, 3,873 represented planted individuals and 347 were wild-growing records indicative of naturalisation. Naturalisation probability, estimated using empirical Bayes shrinkage with Wilson score confidence intervals, was highest for Livistona chinensis , followed by Caryota mitis and Phoenix dactylifera . Seventeen taxa showed evidence of naturalisation, substantially exceeding the four currently recognised for South Africa in the Global Naturalized Alien Flora database. An ensemble habitat suitability model evaluated using spatial block cross-validation (calibration TSS = 0.853, AUC = 0.972) identified the Human Footprint Index and minimum winter temperature as the dominant predictors. A composite naturalisation susceptibility assessment integrating habitat suitability, propagule pressure, and proximity to existing naturalising populations identified 72 high-priority quarter-degree cells concentrated in three urbanised regions. These findings demonstrate the value of citizen science platforms for detecting incipient naturalisation events and a spatially explicit framework for prioritising early detection before invasive palm populations become widespread and costly to control.

title: Anti-Racism in Racial Discrimination Law
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract This chapter inaugurates Part II of the book by locating the concepts considered in the previous chapters—racism and anti-racism—in legal doctrine. It thus serves as a bridge between theory and practice of racism and anti-racism in law. In particular, the chapter explores how racism came to be addressed in law not as such, that is, as racism, but through the prohibition of the category of racial discrimination. It thus traces the development of discrimination law in the UK as the primary vehicle for anti-racism in law—revealing, in the process, the continuities and discontinuities in hoisting the flag of anti-racism on a fitting but frigid mast of discrimination law.

title: Racial Discrimination in Comparative Law
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines how racial discrimination is addressed in comparative law. It focusses on three countries: Canada, India, and South Africa. The interest in looking beyond the UK is to understand whether ‘constitutionalising’ the prohibition of racial discrimination furthers anti-racism any better than statutory and common law. The three comparative jurisdictions chosen here not only address racial discrimination in their statutory law but also constitutional law. In fact, in all three jurisdictions, historical and contemporary discourses in anti-racism have informed constitutional law. These jurisdictions thus prove instructive in appreciating the contours of anti-racism in comparative constitutional law. Nevertheless, the chapter shows that even an explicit recognition of transformative anti-racism in constitutions cannot, by itself, give effect to anti-racism as a legal principle. The minutia of constitutional law doctrine is where anti-racism is put into effect. The chapter seeks to arm the reader with this minutia.

title: Racial Discrimination in International Law
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract This chapter turns to anti-racism in international law. In particular, it considers the extent to which the practice of the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (‘CERD’)—the specialist treaty body tasked with monitoring and enforcing the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (‘ICERD’)—reflects anti-racism as a legal principle. It finds that the pre-eminence of the norm, prohibiting racial discrimination in international law, does not automatically translate into addressing structural racism. It appears that the broader, and less case-specific, the intervention in international law is, the more dynamic its response to structural racism. In contrast, the more particular and case-specific the intervention is, the less its ability to appreciate and address structural racism.

title: Racial Discrimination at Common Law
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines the reception of claims of racial discrimination at common law. Following the previous chapters, it asks, if structural racism is only partially addressed under the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998, where else can we locate claims of structural racism? The chapter traces the lineage of judicial review claims involving racial discrimination and shows that just as the Supreme Court has now confirmed in its 2018 Gallaher decision, that there is no common law principle of equality, there appears to be no clear commitment to anti-racism as a legal principle at common law either. This is despite early signs of a prohibition of racial discrimination developing within rationality review, quite distinctly from a general principle of equality. But the application of the prohibition of racial discrimination at common law has not been consistent and in any case is overshadowed by statutory law. Ultimately, the site of common law appears to be a missed opportunity. However, this chapter argues that, in principle, the nature of common law judicial review holds the normative possibility of addressing structural racism, given that the state is the respondent and the matters concern questions of general importance. Anti-racism as a legal principle could be suitably applied at common law.

title: Racial Discrimination under the Equality Act 2010
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract This chapter examines the doctrine under the primary equality legislation in Britain today—the Equality Act 2010. Almost fifteen years of experience shows that racial discrimination law has hardly operated as a bulwark against racism, especially structural racism. The only points at which it seems to be effective are cases of interpersonal racism that too obvious cases of ‘bald’ racism such as those involving racial slurs, racial bias or racial stereotyping, and prejudice. Cases involving institutional and structural racism and even cases of interpersonal racism which lack smoking gun evidence seldom succeed, though they appear relatively frequently before the courts. The chapter explains discrimination law’s lack of a dynamic response to racism as having to do with four principal limitations to its scope—personal, material, evidential, and remedial. In almost every conceivable way then, doctrinally, the EqA operates as a structure of structural racism rather than its antidote.

title: Racial Discrimination under the Human Rights Act 1998
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract How is racism addressed under the Human Rights Act 1998 (‘HRA’)? This chapter is dedicated to answering this question. The question is fitting in the context of the HRA as it allows challenging the state—its primary and subordinate legislations and actions of public authorities—and thus appears primed to challenge the state’s role in enacting structural racism in principle. Surprisingly therefore, the chapter finds that these challenges seldom succeed, barring a small number of cases. The chapter thus parses through the case law to identify the lines of judicial reasoning which enable or disable redressing structural racism and enacting transformative anti-racism.

title: Contribution of Smallholder Poultry Production to Household Food Security in Billiri Local Government Area, Gombe State, Nigeria

authors: B. B.; I. B.; M. Sanga

abstract: Poultry production can contribute to household food security through direct provision of eggs and meat and through income generated from the sale of birds and poultry products. This study assessed the contribution of smallholder poultry production to household food security in Billiri Local Government Area (LGA), Gombe State, Nigeria. Primary cross-sectional data were collected in 2025 from 160 poultry-farming households selected through a multistage procedure covering Banganje, Billiri, Tanglang and Todi wards. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize households, production systems, institutional access and poultry-related food-security pathways, while the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale (HFIAS) was used to measure household food insecurity. A multiple regression model was used to examine factors associated with the HFIAS score. Poultry production was predominantly small-scale and diversified: 92.5% of respondents kept local chickens and 87.5% kept broilers, while 92.5% reported extensive management. Most households (93.8%) indicated that poultry served both consumption and income purposes. Although direct consumption of own-produced chicken was infrequent, poultry income provided an important indirect food-security pathway: 100% of households reported that poultry income helped them cope with food shortages during the preceding six months, with income used mainly to purchase grains (63.1%) and vegetables (24.4%). Food insecurity was positively associated with household size and negatively associated with education, total household income, poultry-derived income, access to veterinary services and access to credit. The model explained 26.8% of the variation in HFIAS scores. However, the sector was constrained by high feed costs, climate-related risks, inadequate credit and disease outbreaks. Strengthening veterinary services, improving affordable finance and feed access, climate-resilient management, and producer-market linkages could increase the food-security benefits of smallholder poultry production in the study area.

title: Structural Racism, Discrimination and Epigenetics: How Social Inequality May Become Biologically Embedded
source: Advances in Social Sciences Research Journal
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: This article examines the relationship between structural racialisation, discrimination, social inequality, and epigenetic processes, with particular attention to the concept of biological embedding. Rather than conceptualising race as a biological characteristic, the analysis treats racialisation as a socially constructed process through which historical, institutional, economic, and environmental conditions can generate unequal exposures across populations. Social epigenetics provides a potential framework for understanding how socioeconomic disadvantage, neighbourhood conditions, environmental hazards, unequal healthcare access, racialised discrimination, and chronic psychosocial stress may influence physiological regulation, including DNA methylation and measures of epigenetic ageing. The available evidence suggests associations between adverse social conditions and epigenetic measures of biological ageing, although findings vary across populations, exposures, methodologies, and epigenetic clocks. Consequently, epigenetic differences observed between racialised populations should not be interpreted as evidence of inherent biological differences; rather, they may reflect differential exposure to socially structured environments. This perspective shifts the analytical focus from presumed biological differences between populations towards the processes through which racialised social environments create unequal biological exposures and potentially divergent health trajectories. Particular caution is required regarding intergenerational and transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. Although historical racialisation, enslavement, colonialism, socioeconomic inequality, and other forms of adversity can produce consequences extending across generations, current human evidence does not justify assuming that such effects are routinely transmitted through inherited epigenetic modifications. Intergenerational persistence can instead occur through family relationships, socioeconomic resources, neighbourhood environments, cultural memory, institutional arrangements, continuing discrimination, and renewed exposure to adversity in each generation. Epigenetic processes may contribute to these pathways but should not be presumed to constitute their principal mechanism. This article therefore advances a non-deterministic interpretation of social epigenetics: social inequality can become biologically embedded without becoming biologically predetermined. This framework has important implications for research and policy because it locates potential biological inequalities not in racialised populations themselves, but in the unequal social, economic, institutional, and environmental conditions to which populations are differentially exposed.

abstract: Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) is increasingly recognised as essential in research design and funding. While benefits for patients include empowerment and trust in science, PPI also offers unique learning opportunities for early-stage researchers (ESRs), however, structured experiential PPI training for ESRs remains limited. The objective of this work is to report on the impact of a structured PPI engagement event, Be the Voice in Your Community of Health Research on ESRs’ confidence, skills, and understanding of PPI, while supporting patients from diverse ethnic backgrounds to share their lived experiences in cancer care and research. A one-day workshop held in 2025 at University College Dublin (UCD) combined short talks, patient panels and small-group discussions with facilitation. Each facilitation group included one senior researcher, who co-facilitated the session alongside the ESRs. The senior researcher provided oversight, supported discussion flow, and ensured methodological consistency, while the ESRs led participant engagement and interactive components. Participants comprised 5 senior researchers, 10 early-stage researchers (ESRs; PhD students and research assistants working in cancer biology, molecular oncology, bioinformatics and computational biology), and 20 community participants from minority ethnic backgrounds living in Ireland, including three individuals with lived experience of cancer. Post-event reflections and an anonymised questionnaire captured qualitative and quantitative feedback from the ESRs. Descriptive statistics summarised Likert-type items. Qualitative data were thematically analysed. Nine of 10 ESRs rated the event ‘excellent’ (one ‘good’). Self-rated confidence in speaking with patients increased (mean of 4.3 before to 6.0 after; 7-point scale). Qualitative themes indicated (i) development of communication, (ii) active listening and empathy (iii) renewed research motivation and (iv) intention to adopt more inclusive research practices. ESRs showed a desire for more frequent training opportunities of this nature. Community participants reported feeling heard and respected and emphasised the importance of cultural awareness and interpersonal respect. This event demonstrated the dual value of PPI by creating a structured yet informal setting that fostered open dialogue and mutual learning, empowering patients while enriching researchers’ understanding and practice. Embedding structured PPI training early in research careers may help cultivate a generation of empathetic, socially responsible scientists and advance more inclusive, patient-centred cancer research. This paper describes a hands-on training event that brought together early-stage cancer researchers (ESRs) and members of ethnic minority communities. Most researchers know patient and public involvement (PPI) matters, but do not receive practical training. At the ‘Be the Voice of Your Community in Health Research’ event held in 2025, community participants shared real experiences of cancer care and research. Researchers practised listening and communication in small‑group discussions. Feedback showed that both researchers and patients found the experience valuable. Researchers felt more confident and reported a better understanding of patient perspectives while participants felt respected and heard. Face-to-face engagement helped researchers see how their work affects people in everyday life. Offering structured PPI training early in research can make involvement meaningful rather than tokenistic.

title: Putting Eighteenth-Century Ireland Underwater

abstract: This essay looks at eighteenth-century Ireland from an underwater perspective, using blue humanities theory. It explores Ireland’s place in a new emerging sea of blue humanities scholarship, arguing that the eighteenth century marks a lynchpin moment in Ireland’s cultural entanglement with water. At the same time that Catholic inscription in the British navy rose to an all-time high and the penal laws limited tenants’ access to Irish waters, Irish culture also exhibited creative and decolonial ways of thinking with water. While the rest of Western culture was adapting to ‘modern water’, a concept Jamie Linton uses to explain humanity’s conceived social separation from aquatic ecosystems, Irish folklore thought about traditional Irish life in amphibious ways. Lastly, this essay approaches the shipwreck of the French frigate La Surveillante, scuttled in 1796 off Bantry Bay, to consider how Irish culture might hold underwater afterlives. The blue humanities can revitalize the way we think about eighteenth-century Ireland by helping us to see a sunken ship as a new underwater story.

title: From Empire to Deportability: Afghan Asylum Seekers’ Ethnic Fault-Lines and the Politics of “Cricketing Badal” within German’s Asylum Regimes

abstract: Abstract This research study examines the political economy benefits of cricket sport exercised by Afghan asylum seekers in Germany as a tactic to evade deportation and find assimilation into German society. Cricket serves as a platform for asylum seekers to impress German authorities and show a positive image in order to postpone the deportation process. The study argues that ethnic fault-lines among Afghan ethnic groups are prominently displayed within the cricket squad, as each ethnic group attempts to establish superiority over the others. This ethnic superiority struggle and Tarburwali (agnatic rivalry) among asylum seekers are grounded in past political tensions in Afghanistan, exacerbated during the Cold War when the United States backed militant factions opposing the Soviet Union and used ethnic faultlines for their own political economy purposes. Not only the Cold War but in Germany, these pre-existing differences are intensified by the asylum system, like putting asylum seekers in direct competition for residence cards and protection against deportation. In such a way of life,ethnic dominancy in the sphere of cricket to project a positive image in order to integrate immediately. In this case, the cricket team represents the enduring ethnic rivalries and the impact of structural forces in the receiving country, demonstrating how past political contexts and contemporary asylum policies intersect to shape the social dynamics of asylum seekers.

title: Sanitation, Safety, and Stress
source: Navigating Marginality and Agency Among Migrant Women
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Rapid urbanization and migration have increased the number of women living in informal urban settlements with limited access to sanitation and healthcare. This chapter examines how inadequate sanitation affects the physical health, safety, and mental wellbeing of migrant women in urban India. Using intersectionality and feminist public health perspectives, the study explores the ways gender, migration status, and socio-economic vulnerability shape health outcomes. Poor sanitation exposes women to health risks, harassment, and insecurity, contributing to stress, anxiety, and emotional distress. At the same time, migrant women employ coping strategies and community support networks to manage these challenges. By highlighting the link between sanitation, safety, and mental wellbeing, the chapter contributes to discussions on migration, gender, and public health. It also offers policy recommendations for gender-sensitive sanitation services, inclusive urban governance, and improved health interventions for migrant women.

title: Perceptions of medical overuse among health professionals with migrant backgrounds in Norway: a qualitative study
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
authors: Justin Haugland-Pruitt; Stefán Hjörleifsson; Esperanza Diaz
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract Background Medical overuse, defined as the provision of healthcare where potential harm outweighs benefit, is a growing global concern that often coexists with underuse. Migrant health professionals bring experience from healthcare systems shaped by different clinical norms, resource constraints, and understandings of appropriate care. However, little is known about how they interpret concepts such as medical overuse when adapting to the Norwegian healthcare system. This study aimed to explore how migrant health professionals in Norway understand and interpret medical overuse in a new healthcare context. Methods A qualitative study was conducted in Bergen, Norway, using a sequential design combining facilitated group sessions and semi-structured individual interviews. Participants ( n = 7) were highly educated migrants with healthcare backgrounds recruited through the Integration for Health (I4H) intervention programme. Facilitated group sessions introduced the concept of medical overuse and provided a shared conceptual foundation for subsequent interviews. Individual interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using inductive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Medical overuse was unfamiliar to all participants before participation in the study but became recognizable through reflection on prior professional experience. Three themes were identified. First, participants attributed overuse in their home healthcare systems primarily to structural factors, including financial incentives, privatization, weak regulation, and expectations of treatment. Second, most participants experienced tension between prior expectations of care and encounters with the Norwegian healthcare system, often interpreting gatekeeping, diagnostic restraint, and waiting times as indicators of underuse. Third, participants described a process of professional recalibration marked by normative friction between established understandings of appropriate care and Norwegian approaches emphasizing restraint and resource stewardship. Several participants continued to associate extensive testing and intervention with clinical competence despite acknowledging overuse as a legitimate concern. Conclusion Understandings of medical overuse are shaped by professional norms developed within specific healthcare systems and re-evaluated through experiences of migration and professional transition. Differences in healthcare-system structures and expectations of appropriate care may generate normative friction when health professionals encounter new clinical cultures. Efforts to address medical overuse in increasingly diverse healthcare systems should extend beyond guideline dissemination to include explicit engagement with differing professional norms and support for professional adaptation.

title: Alcoholism, Domestic Violence and Murder: Assessing English Sentiments of Irish Immigrants in the Nineteenth Century
source: Transactions of the Historic Society of Lancashire and Cheshire

abstract: The migration and settlement account of the McKerney family in Lancashire from 1855 acts as a case study in this article to reflect on English sentiments towards Irish immigrants in the mid-to-late nineteenth century following the economic hardship caused by the Great Famine. After starting a new life in England free of starvation and disease, several members of the McKerney family suffered from alcoholism, domestic violence, mental illness and crime while living in the slums of Preston’s Irish quarter. This article examines two murder cases involving members of the McKerney family in 1876 and 1887 that symbolised several Irish stereotypes widely circulated during the period, revealing underlying negative sentiments towards the Irish in the ways the authorities investigated the murders and the local press portrayed those involved. The dramatic events in the McKerney family history serve as a springboard to explore broader themes in the history of Irish immigration to England, including the illustration of nuanced points of othering experienced by the Irish.

abstract: Purpose COVID-19 was a global outbreak with long-term consequences. This paper aims to consider protective and vulnerability factors of psychological trauma and moral injury in frontline workers and their families during public health crises (COVID-19) and how resilience can mitigate impact. Design/methodology/approach Study one included interviews with 21 family members of frontline workers and 11 frontline workers. Study two determined the severity of psychological trauma and moral injury, as well as the role of resilience in 203 participants (Frontline workers, n = 98; Families, n = 105). Findings Thematic analysis of Study one highlighted several promotive and protective factors of psychological trauma, moral injury and resilience. Study two explored this in more detail in frontline workers and their families, noting that they experienced moderate levels of moral injury and psychological trauma. Moderate levels of resilience emerged, positively predicted by subjective well-being. Moral injury was found to have a causal effect on psychological trauma via resilience. Originality/value Findings culminated in the development of a conceptual model – the Health Crisis Impact Model (HCIM), which proposes a two-way inter-connected pathway, identifying the impact of stressors specific to public health crises on frontline workers and their families, as well as the protective factors of resilience and how these can promote the development of resilience.

title: Climate Migrants in the Context of Climate Change
source: Contemporary Approaches to Migration, Identity, and Integration
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Climate change, one of the major challenges of our time, has brought with it the debate on climate migration. Over the last century, the number of people migrating due to climate change has been steadily increasing, and it is estimated that millions of people will be displaced by climate change in the coming years. As a result of rising air temperatures, rising sea level, increasing aridity, the depletion of water resources, the dwindling of resources essential for life, and the rise in the number of natural disasters linked to climate change, billions of people are being affected by this situation. It is also a well-known fact that the scale of conflicts and violence is beginning to change as a result of these problems. Consequently, the fact that people's living environments are becoming uninhabitable, coupled with the lack of security resulting from conflicts and acts of violence, is forcing them to migrate to more liveable places.

title: Development and Psychometric Evaluation of the Migrant Health Competency Scale for Nurses
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Aim: This methodological study aimed to develop the Migrant Health Competency Scale for Nurses (MHCSN) and evaluate its validity and reliability. Methods: The study was conducted with a total of 600 nurses, including 301 nurses from Erzurum City Hospital, 225 nurses from Atatürk University Research Hospital, and 74 nurses working in Family Health Centers in Erzurum, Türkiye. Data were collected using a demographic information form and a preliminary 31-item scale. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 22.0 and AMOS. Descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and reliability analyses were performed to evaluate the psychometric properties of the scale. Results: The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy was 0.912, indicating excellent suitability for factor analysis. The final scale consisted of 29 items organized into seven subscales, explaining 55.388% of the total variance. Factor loadings ranged from 0.456 to 0.739. The overall Cronbach's alpha coefficient was 0.902, while the Cronbach's alpha coefficients for the subscales ranged from 0.62 to 0.79, demonstrating acceptable to good internal consistency. Conclusion: The Migrant Health Competency Scale for Nurses (MHCSN) is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing nurses' competencies in migrant health. Future studies are recommended to further evaluate the psychometric properties of the scale in different cultural settings and among more diverse nursing populations.

title: Regional Disparities and Ethnic–Spatial Differentiation: Multidimensional Socio-Economic Deprivation Among Ethnic Minorities in Vietnam
authors: Huong Le Van; Hoang Vo Trong; Le Thi Hong Phuong
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Spatial inequality in multi-ethnic societies may reflect differentiation across both territorial and ethnic contexts. This study examines multidimensional socio-economic deprivation among Vietnam’s ethnic minorities using the 2024 national survey and 189 ethnic–regional combinations representing 14.55 million people. A four-pillar Multidimensional Socio-Economic Deprivation Index (MDI), population-weighted Theil decomposition, and K-means clustering were applied. Population-weighted regional MDI ranged from 0.229 to 0.309, while substantial variation was also observed among ethnic–regional combinations. The total Theil index was 0.0198. In the regional decomposition, between-region differences accounted for 14.0% of total inequality, whereas 86.0% occurred within regions. In an alternative decomposition by ethnicity, the between-ethnicity component accounted for 94.7% of the same total inequality. Housing and Labor–Livelihoods were prominent components of deprivation, while the cluster analysis identified distinct pillar profiles that were not fully represented by aggregate MDI values. These findings show that broad regional averages can conceal substantial ethnic differentiation and within-region heterogeneity. The study supports a diagnostic approach that combines ethnicity-sensitive and place-sensitive information with deprivation profiles, while recognizing that specific interventions require additional assessment of local conditions and implementation capacity.

title: Identifications and Multiple Others: A Case Study of Descendants of Moroccan and Pakistani Migrants in Barcelona
source: Journal of International Migration and Integration
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
reasons: no Ireland reference
empirical_signals: case study, fieldwork, findings, interviews, qualitative
abstract: Abstract This article analyses the negotiation of identifications among children of migrants from the Moroccan and Pakistani diasporas in Barcelona. Drawing on a relational and non-essentialist understanding of identifications, it approaches identifications as socially situated processes of becoming shaped by habitus dispositions, positioning, enabling conditions and interaction. The study is based on qualitative and visual fieldwork with 17 young people in their final year of compulsory education in two public secondary schools located in a highly segregated and superdiverse neighbourhood marked by class homogeneity, heterogeneity of origins and the limited presence of white population. Through 49 interviews in three rounds, including photo-elicitation, the article explores how these young people narrate their relationships with different constitutive others. The findings are organised around three axes: others “from here”, the other others and our others. First, the article shows how “the Catalan” and “the Spanish” are constructed through geographical distance, class distinction, sociolinguistic boundaries and experiences of racist, anti-Muslim and antimoro discrimination. Second, it analyses how, in the absence of a strong presence of groups “from here”, young people establish complex relations of proximity and distance with other migrant-origin groups in the neighbourhood. Third, it examines the production of internal others within their own diasporas, particularly through distinctions between “good” and “bad” migrants. The article argues that school and urban segregation do not merely distribute social groups across space, but also establish the material and symbolic conditions through which situated ways of understanding oneself and others are produced.

title: Irish giants: from myth to medicine.
authors: W. D. de Herder; P. B. Loughrey; M. Korbonits; A. Daly
reasons: migration incidental (1 core-term mention(s), not in title)
abstract: The archetype of the 'Irish giant' in folklore appears to be rooted in historical individuals afflicted by pituitary gigantism. This review compiles and critically assesses the veracity of historical accounts, primarily from the late 17th to the early 20th century, for a group of individuals with gigantism that had Irish origins. Clinical and, in some cases, osteological data (e.g., Charles Byrne, Cornelius Magrath, and Patrick Cotter) confirm a diagnosis of pituitary gigantism, a rare disease that is caused by excess growth hormone secretion from a pituitary adenoma. In the pre-scientific era, the effects of the unopposed hormone excess resulted in extreme tall stature, debilitating morbidity, and usually premature death. This aligns with our modern understanding of the potential severity of hormonal excess and tumour growth in pituitary gigantism. The high concentration of cases in Ulster is explained by a founder germline pathogenic variant (c.910 C > T, p.(R304*)) in the AIP gene, that was identified in multiple contemporary families, later in the skeleton of Charles Byrne and most recently, among the Irish diaspora. Estimated to have arisen around 2500 years ago, this variant established a direct medical explanation for a regional phenomenon. In this review we provide a detailed compilation of historical Irish giants and discuss the evidence linking myth and folklore to the modern medical reality of pituitary gigantism as a rare, severe genetic disease.

abstract:
Research on teachers’ beliefs, education system design, and multilingual education underscore the need for professional
 development and structural reforms to move beyond symbolic inclusion of newly arrived migrant students towards equitable educational
 outcomes. This paper presents an investigation on how immersive and receptive educational systems models influence secondary school
 teachers’ beliefs, practices, and perceptions concerning linguistic diversity and the inclusion of migrant-background students. The study
 draws on survey data from 111 secondary school teachers across five European regions, Spain (Asturias), Ireland, the Netherlands, and
 Belgium (Flanders and Wallonia-Brussels), combining descriptive statistics, non-parametric tests, and thematic analysis of open-ended
 responses. The analysis revealed that while teachers across both system types expressed inclusive intentions, their practices and
 perspectives varied. Across both models, strongly asset-based perspectives were relatively rare, while policy clarity emerged as a key
 factor enabling more consistent inclusive practice. Together, these findings point to meaningful differences in how systemic orientations
 relate to teachers’ understandings and enactments of inclusive pedagogy.

title: Occupational Injuries and Illnesses Under the Employment Permit System: Exploring Perceptions and Responses of Migrant Workers in South Korea
source: Journal of Immigrant and Minority Health
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
authors: Hayoung Lee; Myung-Joo Kang; Seung-Sup Kim
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Abstract The number of migrant workers for temporary labor has rapidly increased, alongside high mortality rates in South Korea. This study explores the occupational safety and health conditions of migrant workers employed under the Employment Permit System (EPS). Data were collected through in-depth interviews with 11 EPS migrant workers who had experienced occupational injuries and illnesses, supplemented by secondary data such as official government guidelines, administrative manuals, and relevant legislation. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The results are as follows: first, regarding migrant workers’ perceptions of the workplace environments that contributed to occupational injuries and illnesses, four subthemes were identified: restricted access to EPS workplace information; assignment to small-scale workplaces; inadequate safety training; and nominally conducted safety inspections. Second, three subthemes emerged regarding the contexts that prevented migrant workers from appropriately responding to their occupational injuries and illnesses: inaccessibility of medical services; institutional barriers to the Workers’ Compensation System; and lack of the right to transfer workplaces. Based on the results, this study highlights the importance of linking occupational health and safety policy with labor migration policy.

title: Hemispheric Exclusions: Racial Borders and ‘Anti‐Black’ Racism Against Haitian Migrants in the Americas
authors: Denise N. Obinna; Amanda Pinheiro de Oliveira
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: ABSTRACT Emigrating from a country beset with political instability, gang violence and severe food shortages, Haitian migrants have sought sanctuary across the Americas. Yet despite their desperate search for asylum, Haitians have had to deal with anti‐Black and anti‐Haitian racism. As a form of hemispheric exclusion, Haitians have encountered racial borders as they attempt to cross international boundaries. Facing challenges due to their irregular status as transient migrants, we assert that the denial of asylum across the Americas represents a systemic form of racialized exclusion. Analysing contexts of reception in Brazil, Mexico and the United States, we explore the complexities of migration for displaced Haitians. Our work also explores the growth of Haitijuana —a community on the San Diego–Tijuana border, which has grown amid exclusionary policies in the United States and Mexico. Our work argues that racial borders perpetuate anti‐Black racism against Haitian migrants. We present a complex study of race, national origin and xenophobia across the hemisphere.

title: Northern France to Ulster: the Lisburn Huguenots revisited
reasons: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: This article reassesses the origins and development of the Huguenot colony established in Lisburn at the turn of the eighteenth century under the leadership of Louis Crommelin. Dispatched to Ireland in 1698 by Henri de Massue de Ruvigny to improve the linen industry, Crommelin settled in Lisburn – with him a group of skilled migrants who formed the core of the colony. Drawing on church records from France, Ireland, the Netherlands and England, this study re-examines the colony’s formation within its broader social, religious and economic contexts. Particular attention is given to the community’s origins in Saint Quentin, northern France, where a shared Protestant identity fostered strong cohesion and shaped patterns of migration. By integrating sources from Saint Quentin, the Netherlands and Lisburn, the study highlights the importance of kinship networks alongside occupational expertise. Migration is shown to have been closely linked to Crommelin’s patronage and extended family connections, which fostered continuity and integration in a new environment. This approach offers a deeper understanding of the community’s origins and reveals previously unexplored relationships, enabling a more precise reconstruction of this distinctive Huguenot micro-diaspora. It further illustrates how migrant communities relied on intertwined kinship and professional networks to facilitate settlement and integration.

title: “New York City has reached its capacity”: Asylum-seekers, housing, and the conjuring of an asylum crisis
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: From 2022 to 2024, some 239,000 migrants (many of them asylum-seekers) arrived in New York City. The city's municipal government referred to the governance of their arrival as an “asylum crisis.” In this context, this article critically examines the “emergency politics” that concerned housing for asylum-seekers and other migrants during this so-called “crisis.” Building on the migration studies literature, I explain this failure through two “critical diagnostics”—what I call “quasi-Malthusian fiscality” and “intersectionalized emergency politics.” Together, these conjured (“constructed”) and governed the “asylum crisis.” In the empirical part of the article, I demonstrate this toxic admixture through a critical analysis of municipal, private sector, and other nonstate discourses, policies, and practices.

title: George Russell Dartnell (1799-1878): an Irish military surgeon in the Victorian empire.
reasons: migration incidental (1 core-term mention(s), not in title)
abstract:
INTRODUCTION
George Russell Dartnell's historical paintings are in Canadian and British national collections. Little is known about his professional life.


METHOD
Contemporary records including Dartnell's papers were used to document his life.


RESULTS
Dartnell was born and educated in Ireland before entering the British Army Medical Department in 1820. As his career took him to the Mediterranean, Ceylon, India, Burma, Canada and Britain, his watercolours recorded the people and landscapes around his postings. In Canada from 1835 to 1843, he organised military medical services, treated civilian patients and created an unusually extensive visual record of Montreal, Penetanguishene, London and the routes between them. His medical publications ranged from compression treatment for femoral aneurysm to commentary on new medical devices, syphilis, small pox, medical privacy and military discipline. As principal medical officer at Chatham during the Crimean War, he had an important liaison role with Queen Victoria when she made three visits to review wounded soldiers. Dartnell highlighted Irish patients and surgeons to the Queen. He also advocated for the welfare of ordinary soldiers and continued his medical reports including a description of a cranial gunshot injury repaired with a silver plate. After army retirement, he operated a private psychiatric asylum in Warwickshire. He began to exhibit his art with the Royal Birmingham Society of Artists.


CONCLUSION
Dartnell's career illuminates the contribution of Irish medical training to nineteenth-century army medicine and the close relationship between clinical observation, administration and visual documentation. In the history of Irish medicine, his career reveals how Irish surgeons exploited opportunities in military surgery and empire.

title: Late HIV diagnosis: An application of flexible Bayesian approaches to understand associated factors and time to diagnosis in Ireland, 2015-2024.
authors: Cian Dowling-Cullen; Katie M. O'Brien; Kate O'Donnell; M. Archibald; P. Downes; D. Field; C. Hurley; Fiona Lyons; E. Muldoon; P. Barrett; Cathal D. Walsh; D. Igoe
reasons: only ambiguous migration terms; MANUAL: no unambiguous migration term; not about migration (checked by title)
abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Late HIV diagnosis is associated with increased morbidity, mortality and onward transmission. The proportion diagnosed late reflects the combined effects of testing delays, incidence and migration, complicating its interpretation. We analysed national HIV surveillance data for Ireland (2015-2024) to understand the factors associated with late HIV diagnosis and testing delays.


METHODS
We estimated prevalence ratios (PRs) for late diagnosis among new diagnoses using Bayesian logistic regression with marginal standardization. We investigated testing delays by estimating infection times and modelling truncation-adjusted delay distributions with Bayesian lognormal regression. We conducted several sensitivity analyses for the main findings.


RESULTS
Among 1551 included new HIV diagnoses with available information, 684 (44.1%) were late. This proportion exceeded 50% in several subgroups, including people aged over 50 years, people whose probable mode of transmission was heterosexual contact, and people born in sub-Saharan Africa. Increasing age (adjusted PR per decade 1.20; 95% credible interval [CrI] 1.15-1.26) and heterosexual transmission (adjusted PR for heterosexual men vs. sex between men 1.43; 95% CrI 1.23-1.67) were associated with late diagnosis in both univariable and multivariable models. For in-Ireland infections, median time from infection to diagnosis was estimated at 1.94 years (95% CrI 1.36-3.40), though this was particularly sensitive to modelling assumptions assessed in our sensitivity analyses, and the multivariable findings suggested longer time to diagnosis for men with heterosexual transmission in particular. For pre-migration infections, median time from arrival to diagnosis was estimated at 0.60 years (95% CrI 0.47-0.83), and an estimated 50.5% of those diagnosed to date were late.


CONCLUSION
Late HIV diagnosis represents a significant challenge. Estimating time-to-diagnosis distributions may help separate the influence of testing delays from incidence and migration. The burden demonstrated across multiple groups highlights the need for normalization and expansion of HIV testing within and beyond traditional risk groups.

authors: Mehmet Akif Okur; Hamza Yavuz; Hüseyin Arif Kınacı

abstract: Abstract Earlier diaspora theory was developed around cases of long-distance dispersal into culturally unfamiliar host societies under conditions of prolonged legal precarity. Bringing Hall’s and Gilroy’s account of hybrid identity into conversation with Grossman’s attribute-based definition of diaspora, this article reads naturalised Syrian-origin Turkish citizens as a case of diaspora-in-becoming. Türkiye is treated as a deviant case and is used in a theory-building mode. Drawing on mixed-methods evidence, the article shows that the sampled naturalised citizens display signs of an emerging diasporic consciousness, whereas institutional consolidation and organised transnational engagement remain limited. Turkish and Syrian orientations coexist within the same lives, but host-society reception shapes whether diasporic consciousness deepens, stabilises or remains thinly organised. The case suggests that the vocabulary of early diaspora theory needs refinement for settings marked by cultural proximity, rapid displacement and accelerated legal incorporation, and that social non-recognition belongs inside the theory of diaspora formation rather than at its margins.

abstract: Objectives The public can directly access dental care by a dental hygienist (DH) in many countries internationally. Research has shown that allowing DHs to work under direct access (DA) improves oral health outcomes, increases service efficiency, and expands access to preventive care. Currently, DA to a DH in Ireland is not permitted. The purpose of this study was to gain a better knowledge of the views of dentists in Ireland in relation to the provision of treatment by DHs under DA in the future. Methods A cross-sectional survey was used on a convenience sample of Irish dentists. The quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, and a thematic analysis was undertaken on the qualitative data. Results Seventy-five dentists completed the survey. Most had experienced working with a DH at some time (97%). Many respondents (65%) felt positive or very positive about the introduction of DA in Ireland. Overall, most respondents felt that all groups of the population (general population, children, people with disabilities, the elderly, people in nursing homes) would benefit from the introduction of DA; the highest perceived benefit was in nursing homes (71%). Conclusions While the concept of DA to DHs was broadly welcomed by dentists practising in Ireland, some reservations and concerns do exist. DA was seen as both an opportunity and a challenge. DA has potential to strengthen the dental care system in Ireland, but its success will depend on thoughtful implementation, updated training pathways, clear regulatory guidance, and alignment with broader workforce planning.

abstract: Abstract Two arguments about ethnic minorities run through the debate over replacing first past the post. One promises that proportional representation would represent minorities better; the other worries that it would empower the parties they have most reason to fear. This article argues that the promise is unreliable and the worry real. Evidence for better descriptive representation rests on women, but that result is driven by party selectorates’ control over candidate selection, not proportionality as such. It does not transfer neatly to ethnic minorities, who differ in number, geographic concentration and a second route into Parliament through ethnic parties. In Britain, the aggregate descriptive gap has largely closed under first past the post. Nor do descriptive gains secure substantive ones. Proportional representation, whether the list system or the single transferable vote, more readily rewards, sustains and amplifies anti‐minority factions, converting intense support into seats and leverage over government. For ethnic minorities, a House of Commons elected through a single‐member ranked‐choice system—which registers not only whom voters prefer first, but also whom they can and cannot accept—is likely to be the best option.

title: Practising Gender Subjectivities in Platform Work: Food Delivery Workers and House Cleaning Workers in China
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: Drawing on interviews from two case studies in China’s food delivery and house cleaning sectors, this research examines workers’ gender subjectivities and their interaction with the labour politics of platform work. Male delivery riders experience a crisis of masculinity, de-flexibilise their labour to maximise income and affirm migrant masculinities, yet their insecurity persists. Female cleaners seek to construct respectable femininities in stigmatised domestic work, juggling care and paid work across life stages and strengthening relational labour to counter algorithmic constraints. The study conceptualises platforms as gendered organisations of flexibility and algorithmic management and examines their interaction with workers’ gendered subjectivities. This interaction produces distinct gendered consequences: exposing men to intensified work and risk of injury, and women to persistent precarity and low pay. The article argues that gender subjectivities both sustain platform domination and provide limited bases for everyday resistance.

title: How Disinformation Turns Protection into a Threat: The Securitisation of Solidarity with Ukrainian Refugees in Romania
source: Analele Universității din Oradea. Seria: Relații Internaționale și Studii Europene
publisher: Department of International Relations and European Studies, University of Oradea
reasons: no Ireland reference
abstract: In times of crisis, public support for refugees can give way to welfare chauvinism and conditional protection. This study analyses how disinformation narratives can erode solidarity with Ukrainian war refugees. Drawing on societal security theory, deservingness research and framing analysis, it develops the concept of the securitisation of solidarity to designate discursive moves that recode humanitarian protection as a threat to the host community's resources, fairness, institutional loyalty, identity or political autonomy. The study combines thematic discourse analysis with systematic content coding of disinformation cases from the Romanian information environment and a comparative layer of narratives circulating beyond Romania. Results show that contestation of refugee protection is voiced predominantly in a distributive register in the Romanian corpus, while criminalisation and cultural othering dominate the comparative corpus. Erosion of solidarity follows a five-move chain from relativising need to delegitimising protection itself. Refuting these narratives required restoring context in all cases, whereas correcting a figure alone never sufficed. Democratic resilience therefore requires institutions not only to correct false claims, but also to make the architecture of protection transparent and address the social precariousness these narratives exploit.
